pr_title: Fixes for NonBacktracking with some combinations of loops and anchors
pr_body:
This PR fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/79116 and some related issues. The problem in the issue was with the pattern `"(a|\b){2}"`, where the alternation inside the loop was not being properly handled. On the input "ac" the proper path is to first match on the `\b` (consuming no input) and only then consuming the `a`. The change to the derivation procedure fixes this by (lazily) unrolling these kinds of contextually nullable loops.

This investigation also uncovered problems in the `PruneLowerPriorityThanNullability` function. The other tests added target these. All of these essentially boil down to not handling the various ways nullability arises in loops. The new `PruneLoop` helper function handles the different cases. Complicating the matter is the fact that nullable parts of a regex cannot be removed even when they are "skipped", since whether capture groups capture zero characters or don't capture at all is a visible behavior. This complication is not a concern in the paper we are publishing, since that doesn't consider captures. @veanes please check the new logic carefully.

Let me know if any of the comments for the various case handlers should be improved, as the arguments are a bit intricate.

The last test, `(\b|a)*`, is a simplified instance of a test that broke in the Rust pattern set while I was developing the fixes, so it could be removed if preferred.

issue_context.title: RegexOptions.NonBacktracking producing wrong matches with loops and contextual nullability
comments:
Tagging subscribers to this area: @dotnet/area-system-text-regularexpressions See info in [area-owners.md](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/docs/area-owners.md) if you want to be subscribed.
Issue Details
### Description `RegexOptions.NonBacktracking` handles patterns like `(a|\b){2}` incorrectly, producing matches of the wrong length. The problem is related to loops with bodies that can accept the empty string, but only contextually due to use of anchors. ### Reproduction Steps ``` using System; using System.Text.RegularExpressions; public class Program { static void Compare(string input, string pattern) { Console.WriteLine($"Testing \"{input}\" with {pattern}"); foreach (Match m in Regex.Matches(input, pattern)) { Console.WriteLine($"Index {m.Index} length {m.Length} with None"); } foreach (Match m in Regex.Matches(input, pattern, RegexOptions.NonBacktracking)) { Console.WriteLine($"Index {m.Index} length {m.Length} with NonBacktracking"); } Console.WriteLine(); } public static void Main() { Compare("ac", @"(a|\b){2}"); } } ``` ### Expected behavior The program should print: ``` Testing "ac" with (a|\b){2} Index 0 length 1 with None Index 2 length 0 with None Index 0 length 1 with NonBacktracking Index 2 length 0 with NonBacktracking ``` ### Actual behavior The program prints: ``` Testing "ac" with (a|\b){2} Index 0 length 1 with None Index 2 length 0 with None Index 0 length 0 with NonBacktracking Index 2 length 0 with NonBacktracking ``` Notice that the first match with NonBacktracking is length 0. ### Regression? This is not a regression, as RegexOptions.NonBacktracking is a new feature. ### Known Workarounds _No response_ ### Configuration .NET 7 on https://dotnetfiddle.net/ ### Other information This problem is due to incorrect logic for handling alternation inside loop bodies. The bug was found by @veanes while proving the correctness of the derivation and pruning rules implemented in the new NonBacktracking feature.

> observe that XZ is nullable because this=(X|Y)Z is nullable

I didn't understand this part.  Why is `(X|Y)Z` nullable?  Is it just that we're only here in this code if `this` node is known to be nullable, and in this example, this is `(X|Y)Z`?

In general, a concatenation `WZ` is nullable **iff** both `W` and `Z` are nullable, so its holds as a direct implication then that both `W=(X|Y)` and `Z` are nullable, therefor if `X` is nullable the so is `XZ`.

To check my understanding, this is only true because:
- `a{0,5}?` is lazy with a lower bound of 0 and thus will first match empty
- `c*` also matches empty

If either of those wasn't true, this reduction would not be possible, yes?  Which of X,Y,Z in your prose aligns with the `c*`?

For example, if the `c*` were instead `c+`, then matching the initial expression against `ac` would require matching the `a` against the first iteration of the `a` from the lazy loop.

The general rule is that in `WZ` if `W` is **high-priority-nullable** (e.g. starts with a lazy loop with lower bound 0 as the first alternative in `W`) then the other alternatives in `W` do not matter and are pruned.

I'm still not understanding. Let's say I have the pattern:
`(a*?|b)c`
I believe what you're saying is the b here can be removed (the alternation is nullable and it starts with a lazy loop with a lower bound of zero). But changing this to `a*?c` changes semantics. If I match against the input "bc", the original would match "bc" whereas the pruned would match only "c". Have I misunderstood?

The expression `(a*?|b)c` is not nullable, the **precondition** is that `WZ` is nullable, meaning `Z` is also nullable, but in your example `c` is not nullable. Above `Z` is some nullable regex, e.g.. `(bc)*`.

> the precondition is that WZ is nullable
